strengths: The paper makes a significant theoretical contribution: it is the first to establish logarithmic regret and O(1/ε) sample complexity for learning ε-Nash equilibria in KL-regularized zero-sum matrix and Markov games, improving over the standard O(√T) rates in prior work.

The algorithmic ideas are novel and technically interesting: leveraging the closed-form Gibbs best-response structure under KL regularization, using best-response sampling, and introducing superoptimistic bonuses for Markov games to handle the unbounded KL terms.

The paper provides a comprehensive theoretical treatment with both regularization-dependent and regularization-independent bounds, and extends to the unregularized setting with a tighter H-dependence.
The problem setup is clearly motivated by modern RLHF/self-play alignment and the connection to KL-regularized games is well explained.
The appendix contains detailed proofs and auxiliary lemmas, showing a serious effort to rigorously establish the claims.
weaknesses: Regret-policy mismatch: The cumulative regret is defined for the sequence (μ_t, ν_t), which are the Nash equilibria of the estimated MSE model, but the algorithm only collects data by executing the best-response pairs (\tilde{μ}_t, ν_t) and (μ_t, \tilde{ν}_t). It never plays or evaluates the policies for which regret is reported. In standard online game/RL regret, this is a conceptual flaw; the objective is closer to a recommendation/exploitability metric than to online regret. The paper should explicitly justify this choice.

Algorithmic error in the min-player projection: In eq. (21c), \Pi_h^-(x) = min{-3(H-h+1)^2, max{x, H-h+1}} is constant equal to -3(H-h+1)^2 for all x, which would make Q^- nonsensical and break the algorithm. The intended clipping is presumably max{-3(H-h+1)^2, min{x, H-h+1}}. The same error appears in the unregularized case (eq. 134c). This is a central algorithmic definition and must be corrected.

Numerous typos and inconsistencies reduce reproducibility: e.g., the bonus definition in C.6, eq. (135), is circular (b^sup := b + 2b^sup); Lemma C.16 states η2 = c4 dH^2 while the surrounding text says η2 = c4 dH; eq. (78) has a duplicated Q^{μ†} and a missing Q^*; there are mismatched parentheses and inconsistent notation throughout the proofs.

The Markov game regularization-dependent bound O(β^{-1} d^3 H^7 log^2 T) is quite loose, and the paper explicitly uses loose bounds in several places (e.g., Lemma C.7). No discussion of tightness or lower bounds is provided, and the extra H factors from superoptimism are not clearly justified as necessary.

For β>0, the regularization-independent Markov game bound is O(d^{3/2} H^3 √T), which is worse by a factor of H than prior unregularized results; the tighter H^2 bound is only established for β=0. This limits the practical appeal of the regularized algorithm.
The computational cost of solving stagewise KL-regularized matrix games for every state in the Markov game is not discussed, which is a significant practical limitation for infinite state spaces.

The related work and reference list contain citation year errors and duplicates (e.g., multiple different Cen et al. entries all labeled 2024, Nash Jr. cited as 2017 for a 1950 paper), indicating a lack of careful proofreading.
No experimental validation is provided. While this is acceptable for a purely theoretical paper, it leaves the practical behavior of the proposed algorithms unexamined.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question: whether KL regularization can yield logarithmic regret in game-theoretic settings, extending single-agent results to two-player zero-sum matrix and Markov games.
Introduces best-response sampling to exploit the closed-form Gibbs best response under KL regularization, circumventing the lack of closed-form NE policies in games.
Proposes the superoptimistic bonus and projection mechanism to handle unbounded KL terms in Markov games, with detailed proof sketches and concentration lemmas.
Provides both regularization-dependent and regularization-independent regret bounds, and derives sample complexities for learning epsilon-NE.
weaknesses: Fundamental mismatch between the regret metric and the algorithm's actual play: the algorithms collect data using optimistic best-response pairs ((tilde mu_t, nu_t) and (mu_t, tilde nu_t)) but the regret is evaluated on the estimated NE policies (mu_t, nu_t), which are never played. In the standard bandit feedback model, every query is an action that incurs regret; here exploration queries are effectively free, so the cumulative regret of the output policies is not the usual online regret. The paper does not define a separate queryable-oracle or pure-exploration protocol to justify this.

The projection operator for the min player in Eq. (21c) is written as Pi_h^-(x) = min{-3(H-h+1)^2, max{x, H-h+1}}, which equals -3(H-h+1)^2 for all x. This would make Q^- constant and break Algorithm 2. It is likely a typo for max{-3(H-h+1)^2, min{x, H-h+1}}, but as written the algorithm is not well-defined.

Numerous notation inconsistencies and typos make the paper hard to verify: b^{max} vs b^{uss} vs b^{use} in Eqs. (23)-(24) and Appendix C.4; D_0^+ and D_0^- are not initialized in Algorithm 1; Eq. (77) contains an apparent typo (Q^{mu-dagger} - Q^{mu-dagger}) inside a squared term; the definition of Pi^- in Eq. (134c) has the same min/max issue.

No assumption is stated on the reference policies (e.g., full support). KL divergences can be infinite if a reference policy assigns zero probability to an action that the current policy puts mass on, which affects the validity of the Gibbs closed-form expressions and the bounded-KL lemmas.

The beta=0 case of Theorem 3.1 is not proved for the same algorithm (with bonus Eq. (24) and projection Eq. (21)). Appendix C.6 introduces a different projection and bonus for beta=0, so the claim of a unified guarantee for any beta>=0 with the main algorithm is not fully supported.

The regularization-independent regret bound for SOMG (O(d^{3/2} H^3 sqrt(T))) is worse than prior work such as VMG (O(d H^{3/2} sqrt(T))), and the regularized bound has very poor dependence on d and H (O(beta^{-1} d^3 H^7 log^2 T)). The paper does not discuss these constant-factor and polynomial-factor drawbacks or when the asymptotic epsilon improvement becomes practically relevant.

The algorithm requires solving a KL-regularized stagewise matrix game for every state at every iteration. For infinite state spaces (allowed in the setup), this is computationally intractable; the paper only mentions extragradient convergence but does not address how to implement the updates in practice.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations section and does not discuss the mismatch between the theoretical metric and practical online interaction, nor the computational and constant-factor limitations of the bounds.

strengths: The paper makes a significant theoretical contribution: it provides the first logarithmic regret guarantees for KL-regularized two-player zero-sum matrix and Markov games, improving over the standard O(√T) rates in prior work.

The proposed algorithms OMG and SOMG are novel, leveraging best-response sampling and (for Markov games) a new concept of superoptimistic bonuses. The analysis carefully exploits the closed-form Gibbs structure of best responses to a fixed opponent policy.

The results are strong and well-quantified: for matrix games, regret min{O(d√T), O(β^{-1}d^2 log^2 T)}; for Markov games, min{O(d^{3/2}H^3√T), O(β^{-1}d^3H^7 log^2 T)}, with sample complexity linear in 1/ε for the regularized case. The paper also recovers prior unregularized rates for β=0 (with a tighter H dependence in the appendix).

The theoretical analysis is detailed and non-trivial, including optimism, a superoptimistic gap condition, and careful handling of the unbounded KL terms via stagewise NE policies. The proofs are provided in extensive appendices.
The work is well-positioned in the literature, connecting to RLHF/self-play and recent single-agent KL-regularized RL results, and clearly articulates the technical challenges overcome.
weaknesses: There is a likely critical typo in the projection operator for the min player in Algorithm 2: Π_h^-(x) = min{-3(H-h+1)^2, max{x, H-h+1}} is constant, which would make Q^- independent of data and break the algorithm. It should likely be a non-constant clipping operator (e.g., max{-3(H-h+1)^2, min{x, ...}}). As written, the algorithm is not reproducible/correct for the min player.

Notation is inconsistent: b^{sup}, b^{uss}, b^{max}, b^{use}, b^{RSE} are used interchangeably; D_0^+ and D_0^- are not initialized; and some equations contain typos (e.g., eq. (78) has Q^{μ†} - Q^{μ†}). This makes the presentation harder to follow and could hinder reproducibility.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations discussion. It does not address the assumption of full-support reference policies (otherwise KL can be infinite), the computational cost of solving a KL-regularized matrix game at every state and horizon, or the large H dependence (H^7) in the regularized Markov game bound.
For small β>0, the regularization-independent Markov game bound is O(d^{3/2}H^3√T), which is worse by a factor of H than the best prior unregularized rate; the tighter H^2 rate is only shown for β=0.
No empirical validation is provided. While this is a theory paper, experiments could help illustrate the practical benefit of the logarithmic regret regime and the superoptimistic bonus design.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and well-motivated problem: provably superior sample efficiency under KL regularization in game-theoretic (self-play / alignment) settings, where prior bandit-feedback analyses only achieved O(sqrt(T)) regret matching the unregularized case.

The core technical idea is sound and novel: because Nash equilibrium policies have no closed form but best responses to a fixed opponent do admit a Gibbs closed form, the authors decompose regret into best-response exploitability terms and analyze each using a bandits/RL view with a fixed opponent policy as part of the environment. This cleanly bypasses the missing NE closed form.

The 'superoptimistic' bonus / projection operator construction (making Q+ exceed the standard optimistic estimate so that the gap property 2|Q+ - bar_Q| >= |Q+ - Q^mu| holds) is a genuinely new algorithmic device, and the paper provides the corresponding concentration, optimism, and gap lemmas (C.1-C.4) with induction arguments that appear internally consistent.

The paper provides two simultaneous guarantees (a beta^{-1}-dependent logarithmic bound and a regularization-independent O(sqrt(T)) bound) and takes their min, which is the correct way to present this kind of result and avoids over-claiming in the small-beta / small-T regime.

The proofs are detailed and mostly self-contained (extensive appendix, explicit constants, explicit bonus/covering-number derivations), and the reduction to single-agent bandits/RL (Appendix D.1) recovers the best known single-agent rates, which is a good sanity check.
The contribution is well-situated against prior work (Table 1) and the writing/organization is clear; the LLM-alignment motivation for KL regularization is compelling.
weaknesses: The logarithmic bound carries very large polynomial factors (beta^{-1} d^3 H^7 for Markov games). The crossover point versus the sqrt(T) bound is T ~ beta^{-2} d^3 H^8 log^4, which is astronomically large for realistic H, d, beta, so the asymptotic improvement is of limited practical reach. The paper does not discuss whether these exponents (especially H^7, H^6 on the bonus terms) are tight or artifacts of the analysis.

The regularization-independent fallback for SOMG (d^{3/2} H^3 sqrt(T)) is strictly worse than the prior regularized bound of Yang et al. [2025a] (d H^{3/2} sqrt(T)); thus even outside the log-regime SOMG does not match the state of the art, and the min-over-bounds presentation partly masks this.

The strong-concavity/strong-convexity mechanism that yields the logarithmic rate relies on the KL term being strongly convex, which implicitly requires the reference policies to have (effectively) full support; this is never stated as an assumption and would be needed for the perturbation-stability lemma C.13 and for the beta^{-1} rates. The theorem statements say 'any reference policies,' which is stronger than what the analysis appears to support.

Several decisive steps are hard to verify from the manuscript as given and would benefit from a more careful exposition: the mean-value-theorem monotonicity arguments (eqs. 44, 56) that show G_1 is increasing and G_2 is decreasing in Gamma, and the covering-number derivations (Lemmas C.10-C.11) whose constants feed directly into the regret bounds. No independent numerical or even synthetic verification is provided.

The significance claim ('first to establish logarithmic regret ... in any KL-regularized game-theoretic setting') is plausible but relies on the reader trusting that the intricate induction (superoptimistic gap) and the H^7 accounting are correct; the paper would be stronger with a clearly isolated statement of the key technical theorem (superoptimistic gap) and a discussion of how the H-dependence could be tightened.

As a purely theoretical paper with no experiments, there is nothing to independently reproduce beyond the proofs; this is acceptable for the venue, but combined with the large constants it limits confidence that the bound is meaningful rather than merely correct.

strengths: The paper tackles a novel and significant problem: achieving logarithmic regret in KL-regularized two-player zero-sum matrix and Markov games, extending prior logarithmic-regret results from single-agent settings. The claimed sample complexity linear in 1/ε for finding an ε-NE is a strong theoretical advance.

The algorithmic ideas are well-motivated: leveraging best-response sampling to obtain closed-form Gibbs policies despite the lack of closed-form Nash equilibria, and introducing superoptimistic bonuses to handle unbounded value functions in KL-regularized Markov games.

The theoretical analysis is extensive and addresses several technical challenges, such as the absence of closed-form NE policies and the need to bound covering numbers for the induced superoptimistic value function class.
weaknesses: Critical error in the definition of the projection operator for the min-player's superoptimistic Q-function (eq. 21c). As written, $\Pi_h^-(x) = \min\{-3(H-h+1)^2, \max\{x, H-h+1\}\}$ always equals $-3(H-h+1)^2$ because the maximum is at least $H-h+1$ (positive) while the minimum is negative. This makes $Q^-$ a constant, so the min-player's best response becomes the reference policy $\nu_{\mathrm{ref}}$, eliminating exploration for the min player and breaking the algorithm and its regret guarantees. The correct operator is likely $\max\{-3(H-h+1)^2, \min\{x, H-h+1\}\}$.

Pervasive notation inconsistencies make the paper extremely difficult to verify. The same quantity is denoted $b^{\max}$, $b^{\mathrm{non}}$, $b^{\mathrm{msa}}$, and $b^{\mathrm{mse}}$ in different places (e.g., eq. 23 vs. eq. 24 vs. Lemma C.1 vs. Corollary C.1). The definition of $\eta_1$ in eq. 24 differs from that in Lemma C.1. These inconsistencies obscure the algorithm and the proof.

The proof of the min-player terms $T_7$ and $T_8$ in the Markov game (Theorem C.1) is omitted; the authors merely state that it follows by symmetric arguments. Given the complexity of the superoptimistic gap and the projection operators, this is a significant gap in a 60-page appendix.

The presentation is dense and contains many minor errors: inconsistent use of $\hat{\mu}_t$ vs. $\tilde{\mu}_t$ in the matrix game proofs, missing equation references, and unclear constants. These issues impede reproducibility and make it hard to trust the technical details.

The paper claims to be the first to achieve logarithmic regret in KL-regularized game-theoretic settings, but does not thoroughly discuss concurrent or closely related work that might also claim similar results. A more careful positioning would strengthen the claim.

The Markov game regret bound has very high dependence on $H$ ($H^7$) and $d$ ($d^3$), and the superoptimistic bonus is large (order $d H^2$). While not incorrect, this reduces the practical appeal and suggests the analysis may be loose.

strengths: The paper makes a significant theoretical contribution by establishing the first logarithmic regret guarantees for KL-regularized two-player zero-sum matrix games and Markov games, improving over the standard O(sqrt(T)) rates in prior work.

The algorithmic ideas are novel and technically sound: best-response sampling for matrix games and super-optimistic bonuses with tailored projection operators for Markov games effectively handle the unbounded value functions caused by positive KL regularization terms.

The analysis is rigorous and detailed, with complete proofs in the appendix. The proof mechanisms, such as converting linear bonuses to squared bonuses via strong convexity/concavity, are clearly explained and appear correct.
The results imply sample complexities that scale linearly in 1/epsilon for the regularized setting, which is a substantial improvement and directly relevant to game-theoretic alignment and RLHF.

The paper connects well to practical applications (e.g., LLM alignment via self-play) and provides a reduction to single-agent settings that recovers known bounds, demonstrating the generality of the framework.
weaknesses: The Markov game regret bound has very high polynomial dependence on the horizon (H^7) and dimension (d^3), and the regularization-independent sqrt(T) bound is worse than prior work (Yang et al., 2025a) by factors of d^{1/2} H^{3/2}. This limits the practical relevance of the fallback guarantee.

The stability lemma used for covering number bounds (Lemma C.13) assumes reference policies have full support, but the main theorems claim results for arbitrary reference policies. This gap should be explicitly addressed or the assumption stated.
The paper lacks experimental validation. While this is a theoretical contribution, empirical demonstrations or discussions of practical implementability would strengthen the work.

The presentation is dense and notation-heavy, with several typographical errors (e.g., 'Explotaibility', 'leafing', missing parentheses in algorithm pseudocode). The main text could better highlight the key proof mechanisms and the intuition behind the super-optimistic bonus.

The limitations of the approach, such as the high H dependence and the requirement for solving regularized matrix games at each state, are not thoroughly discussed. A dedicated limitations section would be beneficial.
